point_one.role: Serve as the counterintuitive exception that challenges the shortcut “fruit equals low humidity.” Use strawberries and citrus to show that moisture loss—not the fruit-versus-vegetable label—is the more reliable sorting question.
point_one.new_listener_takeaway: Listeners should ask whether a food rapidly loses water before choosing a drawer setting: strawberries and oranges can favor high humidity, with UC Davis listing an optimal humidity of 90–95% for both. This gives them a mechanism-based rule rather than a simple produce-category rule.
point_one.evidence_anchor: FACT-03: strawberries and citrus such as oranges favor high humidity, while the broader guidance is based on whether food releases ethylene or loses moisture quickly; UC Davis provides the 90–95% humidity figures.
point_one.why_it_matters: This prevents listeners from automatically putting all fruit in the low-humidity drawer and unintentionally drying out produce that needs moisture retention.
point_one.must_not_overlap_with_full_story: Do not repeat the basic definitions of the two drawer settings, the ventilation mechanism, or the standard examples of leafy greens and ethylene-producing foods; those are the main story’s foundation.
point_one.must_not_overlap_with_other_point: Do not discuss foods that should be stored outside the refrigerator; Point Two will handle that storage boundary.

point_two.role: Provide the practical boundary for the advice: before assigning food to a crisper drawer, first decide whether it belongs in the refrigerator at all. Use tomatoes, bananas, and separately the cool, dry-storage group to show where the drawer rule stops applying.
point_two.new_listener_takeaway: Tomatoes and bananas should be kept at room temperature, such as on the counter, rather than placed in either crisper drawer. Potatoes, sweet potatoes, onions, and garlic do not require refrigeration and should be kept in a cool, dry environment—not automatically treated as counter items in exactly the same way.
point_two.evidence_anchor: FACT-04: Iowa State Extension recommends counter storage for tomatoes and bananas, while describing potatoes, sweet potatoes, onions, and garlic as needing a cool, dry environment without refrigeration.
point_two.why_it_matters: This keeps listeners from treating the humidity slider as a universal solution and turning otherwise correct drawer guidance into incorrect storage advice.
point_two.must_not_overlap_with_full_story: Do not repeat how high and low humidity work or the ordinary matching of ethylene-producing foods with low humidity and wilting-prone foods with high humidity; those belong to the main explanation.
point_two.must_not_overlap_with_other_point: Do not focus on strawberries, citrus, or the moisture-loss test; Point One owns the exception that makes produce category an unreliable shortcut.
